a: Jacob settled in the land where his father had lived as a foreigner
t: The Joseph story picks up again
p: This verse is Genesis 37:1, word for word in the Plain English Translation. The story of Joseph's sale was told at 34:10-11.
b: Jubilees told how Joseph was sold in 34:10-11, tying it to the Day of Atonement. Now it returns to Genesis 37:1-2 and moves straight to Egypt. It leaves out Joseph's two dreams, the robe and the brothers' plot in the field (Genesis 37:3-35). Where the Ge'ez says what Genesis says, this translation uses the site's Genesis wording, as here.

a: a eunuch of Pharaoh's
p: The Ge'ez word means a eunuch. Genesis's Hebrew word saris can mean a eunuch or simply a court official.
b: Genesis 37:36 calls Potiphar "a court official of Pharaoh who commanded the bodyguard" (Genesis 37:36). The Hebrew saris came to mean a palace official, whether or not he was castrated, and the Greek translation of Genesis renders it spadōn, a eunuch. The Ge'ez here has the plain word for a eunuch, as in 39:14 for the cupbearer and baker. Jubilees does not comment on how a eunuch could have a wife (39:5). It simply keeps the word it had.

a: the chief of the cooks
p: Genesis's title sar hattabbachim can mean chief cook or captain of the guard. The Ge'ez takes it as chief cook.
b: The Hebrew title in Genesis 37:36 and 39:1 is built on a word for slaughtering, used of butchers and cooks and also of executioners. Most English Bibles, and the site's Genesis, take it as the commander of the king's bodyguard. The Ge'ez liqä mäbsəlan means the head of the cooks, the sense the Greek translation of Genesis also gives. Charles 1902 (page 223) points back to the same title at 34:11, where Potiphar is also called a priest.

a: He put Joseph in charge of his whole house
p: Verses 3-4 shorten Genesis 39:2-6 and say the Lord's blessing twice, as Genesis does.
b: Genesis 39:2-6 says four times that the Lord was with Joseph or blessed the house for his sake. Jubilees keeps the point in two verses. The formula "the Lord made everything he did succeed" comes back at 39:12, as it does in Genesis 39:23, framing the whole chapter: in a rich house or in prison, the Lord is with Joseph.

a: very handsome to see
p: The Ge'ez says Joseph's looks were fine twice over. Charles thought one phrase was copied twice by mistake.
b: The Ge'ez reads "Joseph was good in his appearance, and very handsome was his appearance." Charles 1902 (page 223) suspected a dittography, a phrase written twice by a copyist. It may also be deliberate emphasis, since Genesis 39:6 itself uses two words for Joseph's looks. The Plain English Translation keeps both.

a: the words his father Jacob used to read aloud from the words of Abraham
t: Joseph knew the law before Sinai
p: Genesis has Joseph refuse because it would wrong his master and God. Jubilees adds that he remembered Abraham's written commands.
b: In Genesis 39:8-9 Joseph refuses because his master trusts him and because it would be "great evil" and sin against God. Jubilees keeps the fear of God but adds a written law: Abraham's commands against sexual sin (20:4; 25:7), which Jacob read aloud to his family. This is one of the book's main ideas: the fathers kept God's laws long before Moses. Goes beyond the Bible: Genesis never says Abraham left written commands. Charles 1902 (page 223) notes a related Jewish story in the Talmud (Sotah 36b): the image of Jacob appeared at the window and urged Joseph to stay faithful.

a: A sentence of death has been decreed for that man in the heavens
p: The law of Moses also sets death for adultery. Jubilees says the sentence was decreed in heaven before any law was given on earth.
b: Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22 set the death penalty for a man and a married woman who commit adultery. Agrees with those laws on the penalty. Goes beyond them in its claim that the sentence already stood "in the heavens before the Lord Most High" in Joseph's day. That is the book's picture of law: it is written in heaven first, then revealed, partly to the fathers and fully to Moses.

a: the eternal books
p: Sins are entered into "eternal books" kept before God, an idea shared with Daniel, Malachi and Revelation.
b: The picture of heavenly books where deeds are written runs through the Bible: books opened at the judgment (Daniel 7:10; Revelation 20:12), a book of remembrance (Malachi 3:16), and the book of life (Exodus 32:32-33). Jubilees uses it often for the record of sins and of righteous deeds. Here the point is that a sin done in secret in an Egyptian house is still on record before God.

a: broke through the door
p: Genesis has no locked doors. In Jubilees the woman shuts the doors and Joseph breaks one to escape.
b: In Genesis 39:11-12 the house is simply empty of servants, and Joseph runs out leaving his garment. Jubilees adds that she shut the doors and that he broke through one. The broken door then becomes part of the case against him (39:10-11): the master sees the garment and the door. Goes beyond the Bible in a small way that makes the story tighter: the forced door looks like proof of violence, though it was proof of flight.

a: the one you love
p: The wife reminds her husband how much he loves the slave. Genesis has her blame her husband for bringing him in.
b: In Genesis 39:17 the wife accuses her husband of bringing in "that Hebrew servant" to toy with them. Jubilees' version is shorter and colder: "your Hebrew servant, the one you love." Both versions turn the master's trust, the reason for Joseph's rise, into the weapon against him.

a: He stayed there two years
p: Jubilees puts two years here, before the cupbearer and baker come. Genesis puts two full years after their dreams.
b: Genesis 41:1 says Pharaoh dreamed "at the end of two full years" after the cupbearer was freed. Jubilees places two years in prison before the officials arrive (39:13-14), and later says Joseph spent three years in prison in all (46:3). The book cares about exact time: every event has its year, and the years add up across the whole story of Joseph (see 40:11-12).

a: The two of them had dreams
p: Jubilees gives no vine, no grapes and no baskets of bread. Genesis 40 tells both dreams in full.
b: Genesis 40:5-19 is one of the Bible's fullest dream scenes, with Joseph's words "Don't interpretations belong to God?" (Genesis 40:8). Jubilees reduces it to three verses and leaves out the dreams themselves. The book often shortens stories that teach no law or calendar point and slows down for those that do, such as Judah and Tamar in chapter 41.

a: the baker he hanged
p: The Ge'ez verb means to hang or to crucify. Charles's English has "slew"; Genesis 40:22 says he "hanged" the baker.
b: The verb säqälä is the Ge'ez word for hanging someone up; Dillmann's Lexicon linguae aethiopicae gives both "hang" and "crucify" as its senses. Charles's English (1913) gives the general "slew." The Plain English Translation keeps the specific sense, which matches Genesis 40:19 and 40:22.

a: because he forgot
p: Genesis 40:23 says it twice: he did not remember Joseph, he forgot him. Jubilees says it twice too.
b: Genesis 40:23 ends the prison story with a double statement of forgetting. Jubilees keeps the doubling ("he did not remember... because he forgot") and adds that Joseph had told him what would happen, which makes the forgetting worse. Joseph's own request, "keep me in mind" (Genesis 40:14), is not in Jubilees.

a: about a famine that was coming on the whole land
t: The meaning told before the dream
p: Jubilees names the dreams' subject at once and never describes the cows or the grain.
b: Genesis 41:1-7 and 41:17-24 tell Pharaoh's dreams twice, with seven fat and seven thin cows and seven full and seven thin ears of grain. Jubilees tells the reader at once that the dreams were "about a famine," and never describes them. The narrator, the angel speaking to Moses, already knows the outcome and goes straight to it.

a: his two dreams were one
p: This is Joseph's key line in Genesis 41:25-26: two dreams, one message.
b: Joseph's answer follows Genesis 41:25-31 closely: the two dreams are one, seven years of plenty, then seven years of famine worse than any before. Jubilees leaves out Joseph's words that God, not he, gives the answer (Genesis 41:16) and that God has decided the matter (Genesis 41:32). It brings God back in 40:5, where the Lord gives Joseph favor.

a: the spirit of the Lord is with him
p: Genesis 41:38 has Pharaoh call Joseph a man with "the spirit of God in him." The Ge'ez says the spirit of the Lord.
b: In Genesis Pharaoh asks, "Can we find anyone like this, a man who has the spirit of God in him?" (Genesis 41:38). Jubilees puts it as a statement and uses the book's usual word for God, ʾƎgziʾabḥer, "the Lord." Ge'ez has no separate word for the divine name YHWH, so the Plain English Translation of Jubilees writes "the Lord" throughout, never "the LORD."

a: Pharaoh's second chariot
p: Verses 6-7 follow Genesis 41:40-44: second in the kingdom, the chariot, the linen, the gold chain and the ring.
b: All the signs of office in Genesis 41:40-44 are here, in a slightly different order. Genesis has the ring first, then the linen and chain, then the chariot and the cry. Jubilees has the chariot first and the ring last.

a: fine linen
t: A Greek word in the Ge'ez
p: The Ge'ez word for fine linen is bisos, the Greek byssos.
b: The Ge'ez has bisos, a borrowing of the Greek byssos, fine linen; the Greek Genesis dresses Joseph in a robe of byssos at 41:42. The Ge'ez Jubilees has other borrowed Greek words, such as ṭerebentos "terebinth" in 42:20.

a: El El wa Abirr
p: A Hebrew cry kept in Ge'ez letters. Charles read it as "God, God, the mighty one of God," an expansion of Genesis's "Abrek!"
b: In Genesis 41:43 the people shout a word, "Abrek!", whose meaning is debated. Jubilees has a longer cry, written in Ge'ez letters. Charles 1902 (page 226) reads it as Hebrew 'el 'el wa'abirer, "God, God, the mighty one of God," and suggests that "mighty one of God" was a title for a great wonder-worker. He compares a late text that he calls "The History of Asenath," where Joseph is called "the mighty one of God," and Acts 8:10, where Simon the magician is called "the great power of God." The Latin version has Elel et Habirel.

a: he took no bribes
p: Jubilees praises Joseph as an honest judge: no pride, no favoritism, no bribes. Genesis does not describe his character in office.
b: These virtues are the ones the law of Moses asks of judges: no favoritism and no bribes (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19). Goes beyond the Bible by turning Joseph into the ideal ruler of a foreign land, loved by Pharaoh's whole court. For Jewish readers living under foreign kings, this was a picture of how one of their own could serve a pagan ruler faithfully.

a: there was no satan and no evil
p: The Ge'ez säyṭan comes from the Hebrew satan, "adversary." Jubilees uses the same phrase for times of blessing (23:29; 46:2).
b: Jubilees describes the best times with the words "no satan and no evil": the age of renewal (23:29), and Israel's years in Egypt while Joseph lived (46:2). The Hebrew word satan means an adversary or accuser, and in the Bible it is used both of human enemies (1 Kings 5:4) and of the accuser in heaven (Job 1:6). Here it may mean no enemy at all, or no evil power stirring up trouble. The Plain English Translation writes it in lowercase to leave both open. Jubilees' own name for the leader of the evil spirits is Mastema (10:8).
orig: ወአልቦ ፡ ሰይጣነ ፡ ወአልቦ ፡ እኩየ (wäʾälbo säyṭanä wäʾälbo ʾəkuyä)

a: Sephantiphans
p: Genesis 41:45 has Zaphenath-paneah. The Ge'ez form Sephantiphans came through the Greek.
b: Charles 1902 (page 227) identifies Sephantiphans with the Hebrew of Genesis 41:45, which the site renders Zaphenath-paneah. He notes that Jewish tradition took the name to mean "revealer of secrets," as the Aramaic Targum Onkelos, the Targum called Pseudo-Jonathan and the Syriac translation render it.

a: the daughter of Potiphar
t: Joseph marries his old master's daughter
p: Jubilees treats Potiphar, Joseph's master, and Potiphera, his father-in-law, as one man. Genesis keeps two names.
b: Genesis names Joseph's master Potiphar (Genesis 39:1) and his father-in-law Potiphera, "priest of On" (Genesis 41:45). Jubilees makes them the same person: the chief of the cooks is also the priest of Heliopolis (see 34:11; 44:24). Charles 1902 (page 227) says Origen knew this view and called its source apocryphal. He also notes that later Jewish tradition was troubled that Joseph married a pagan priest's daughter, and the Targum called Pseudo-Jonathan makes Asenath a daughter of Dinah by Shechem. Goes beyond the Bible and does not explain how the woman who accused Joseph is now his mother-in-law.

a: the priest of Heliopolis
p: Genesis calls the city On. Heliopolis, "sun city," is its Greek name.
b: On was the great city of the sun god near modern Cairo. Its Greek name Heliopolis means "city of the sun." The Greek Genesis already writes "priest of Heliopolis" for "priest of On" in 41:45, and the Ge'ez takes the Greek name. Jeremiah 43:13 calls the city Beth-shemesh, "house of the sun."

a: when he stood before Pharaoh
p: Genesis 41:46 also gives Joseph's age as thirty. The phrase "when he stood before Pharaoh" comes twice in the Ge'ez.
b: Genesis 41:46 says Joseph was thirty when he stood before Pharaoh. Joseph was seventeen when sold (39:2), so thirteen years have passed: by the book's own account, ten as a slave and three in prison (46:3). Charles 1902 (page 227) bracketed the repeated clause as a copying slip. The Plain English Translation keeps it, as VanderKam's Ge'ez text has it.

a: In that year Isaac died
p: Genesis tells of Isaac's death in 35:29, before the Joseph story. Jubilees places it in the year Joseph rose to power.
b: Genesis closes Isaac's life in 35:28-29, but it does not say his death came before Joseph was sold. Its numbers allow Jubilees' date. Isaac was sixty when Jacob was born (Genesis 25:26), and Jacob was a hundred and thirty when he came to Egypt (Genesis 47:9), after seven years of plenty and two of famine. So Jacob was about a hundred and twenty-one when Joseph stood before Pharaoh, and Isaac would have been about a hundred and eighty-one. Genesis 35:28 gives Isaac a hundred and eighty years. This is our arithmetic from Genesis; Jubilees simply states the date.

a: one measure of seed yielded eighteen hundred measures
p: Genesis says the land produced "by the handful." Jubilees gives a number far beyond any real harvest.
b: Genesis 41:47 says the land produced abundantly. Isaac's blessed harvest was "a hundred times what he sowed" (Genesis 26:12), and Jesus' parable speaks of thirty, sixty and a hundredfold (Matthew 13:8). Jubilees' eighteen hundredfold is far beyond these, a way of saying that the years of plenty were God's direct gift.

a: In the forty-fifth jubilee, in the second week, in its second year
p: By the book's own count of 49-year jubilees and weeks of years, this is year 2165 after creation.
b: Jubilees dates every event in jubilees of 49 years, each divided into seven weeks of years. Forty-four full jubilees (2,156 years), plus one full week (7 years), plus 2 years gives 2165. Charles 1902 prints the same figure in his margin; it is his calculation, not part of the text. The story of Judah and Tamar is placed here, in the middle of the seven years of plenty, because it is set by date, not where Genesis 38 places it, before Joseph's rise.

a: from the daughters of Aram
p: Genesis never says where Tamar came from. Jubilees makes her an Aramean, a relative of Abraham's family.
b: Abraham's family came from Aram, and Rebekah, Leah and Rachel were all Arameans. By giving Tamar this origin, Jubilees makes her a fit wife for Judah's son, unlike Judah's own Canaanite wife (41:2; 34:20). Charles 1902 (page 228) quotes the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs (Testament of Judah 10), which also calls Tamar "from Mesopotamia, a daughter of Aram." Goes beyond the Bible. Matthew 1:3 names Tamar among Jesus' ancestors without saying where she was from.

a: because his mother was one of the daughters of Canaan
t: Why Er would not lie with Tamar
p: Genesis says only that Er was evil. Jubilees explains his evil: he wanted a Canaanite wife like his mother.
b: Genesis 38:7 gives no details of Er's sin. Jubilees supplies one that fits its strongest theme: marriage with Canaanites is forbidden (20:4; 25:1-3; 30:7). Er hates his Aramean wife and wants one from his mother's people, and his father refuses. The Testament of Judah 10, quoted in Charles 1902 (page 228), tells the same story and blames Er's mother. Goes beyond the Bible.

a: do a brother-in-law's duty for her
p: Genesis 38:8 uses the Hebrew verb for a brother-in-law's duty, later laid down as law in Deuteronomy 25:5-10.
b: When a man died without a son, his brother was to marry the widow and raise a son in the dead man's name (Deuteronomy 25:5-10). Judah's words in Genesis 38:8 use the Hebrew verb for this duty, and Charles 1902 (page 228) notes that the Ge'ez renders the same idea. Jubilees, which usually shows the fathers keeping the laws, does not comment on this one; its law in this chapter is about burning (41:25-26).

a: spilled his seed on the ground
p: Jubilees follows Genesis 38:9-10 closely here: Onan refuses to give his brother a son.
b: As in Genesis 38:9-10, the wrong is that Onan used his brother's widow while refusing to give his dead brother an heir. The Testament of Judah 10, as quoted in Charles 1902 (page 228), adds that he acted at his mother's command.

a: Bedsuel
p: Judah's wife is "Shua's daughter" in Genesis 38:2, 12. Jubilees gives her a name, Bedsuel (34:20).
b: Genesis calls Judah's wife only "the daughter of a Canaanite man whose name was Shua" (Genesis 38:2) and "Shua's daughter" (Genesis 38:12); Hebrew bat-shua means "daughter of Shua." 1 Chronicles 2:3 uses the same words. Charles 1902 (page 228) explains Bedsuel as a form of Bath-shua. Jubilees named her among the brothers' wives at 34:20.

a: would not let her son Shelah marry her
p: In Genesis, Judah holds Shelah back. Jubilees blames his Canaanite wife.
b: Genesis 38:11 and 38:14 make Judah responsible: he feared that Shelah would die like his brothers, and Tamar saw that she had not been given to him. Jubilees moves the blame to Bedsuel, Judah's Canaanite wife, as the Testament of Judah 10 also does (Charles 1902, page 228). This softens Judah's fault and fits the book's view of Canaanite wives. Differs from Genesis in who is responsible.

a: made herself beautiful
p: The Hebrew of Genesis 38:14 says she covered herself. The Greek, Syriac and the Targum Onkelos say she adorned herself, as Jubilees does.
b: Charles 1902 (page 229) notes that Jubilees agrees here with the Septuagint, the Syriac and the Targum Onkelos of Genesis 38:14, which say Tamar adorned herself, against the Masoretic Hebrew "covered herself." The Greek Genesis reads ekallōpisato, "made herself beautiful." The Testament of Judah 12 also has her dressed in bridal finery. Jubilees has both: the veil and the adorning.

a: sat in the gate beside the road to Timnah
p: Genesis says she sat "at the gateway of Enaim." Jubilees has only "the gate beside the road to Timnah."
b: Genesis 38:14 and 38:21 name a place, Enaim ("two springs"). Jubilees drops the name and keeps the gate on the road to Timnah.

a: the ring on my finger, my necklace, and the staff in my hand
p: Genesis has a seal, its cord and a staff. Jubilees has a ring, a necklace and a staff, close to the Greek Genesis.
b: In Genesis 38:18 Judah gives "your seal and your cord, and your staff." A man's seal often hung on a cord around his neck. Charles 1902 (page 229) notes that the Greek Genesis has "ring, cord, staff," and that the Testament of Judah 12 has "staff, belt and royal diadem." Jubilees' "necklace" is the cord, and its "ring" is the seal worn as a signet ring. In Jubilees Judah offers the pledge himself; in Genesis Tamar asks for it.
orig: ሕልቀት ፡ ዘአጽባዕትየ ፡ ወድጕልማየ ፡ ወበትርየ (ḥəlqät zäʾäṣbaʿtəyä wädgʷəlmayä wäbätrəyä)

a: Where is the prostitute who was here?
p: Genesis 38:21-22 has the Adullamite ask for a qedeshah, a "holy woman." Jubilees uses its ordinary word for a prostitute.
b: In Genesis the narrator calls Tamar a prostitute (38:15) but the Adullamite asks for a qedeshah, "holy woman" (Genesis 38:21-22), a word for a woman connected with a shrine. Jubilees uses zämawit, its ordinary word for a prostitute, throughout. Charles 1902 (page 229) notes that the Testament of Judah 12 renders the Genesis word with a Greek term for a woman initiated into the rites of Aphrodite.

a: pregnant from prostitution
p: Genesis 38:24 also has the news reach Judah about three months later.
b: The report follows Genesis 38:24. Jubilees says "when she had finished three months," the same span. In both, the men around Judah call it prostitution, though Tamar was a widow promised to Shelah.

a: let them burn her
p: The law of Moses sets burning for a priest's daughter who becomes a prostitute. Readers explain Judah's sentence in different ways.
b: Leviticus 21:9 says of a priest's daughter who becomes a prostitute, "She is to be burned in fire" (Leviticus 21:9). Charles 1902 (page 230) notes that Rabbi Meir, in Genesis Rabbah 85, made Tamar a daughter of Shem, whom the rabbis identified as a priest, so that law applied to her; the Targum called Pseudo-Jonathan also calls her a priest's daughter. Jubilees gives its own reason: Abraham had commanded burning for sexual sin (20:4; 41:28), and later the book sets burning for a woman given to a foreigner (30:7). Genesis itself gives no reason.

a: she has done something unclean in Israel
p: The phrase recalls Genesis 34:7, where Shechem did "a disgraceful thing in Israel."
b: Jubilees speaks of Israel as a holy people already in Jacob's family. Judah's words echo the brothers' anger at Shechem, "a disgraceful thing in Israel" (Genesis 34:7), and Jubilees' law in 30:7, "shame in Israel" for giving a daughter to a foreigner. Genesis 38 has no such phrase.

a: Tamar is more in the right than I am
p: Genesis has Judah add, "because I never gave her to my son Shelah." Jubilees drops this, because it blamed Bedsuel (41:7).
b: In Genesis 38:26 Judah says Tamar is more in the right "because I never gave her to my son Shelah" (Genesis 38:26). Jubilees keeps the first half and drops the reason. It has already said that Judah's wife, not Judah, kept Shelah from Tamar (41:7). The Ge'ez ṣädqät is from the root for righteousness.

a: she was not given to Shelah
p: Genesis does not say this. Jubilees adds that Tamar was never given to Shelah afterward, because she had been with his father.
b: Genesis 38:26 says only that Judah "did not lie with her again." Jubilees adds that for this reason she was not married to Shelah: she had become forbidden to Judah's family as his partner. Charles 1902 (page 230) quotes the Testament of Judah 12, "nor did I come near her again until my death." Goes beyond the Bible.

a: Perez and Zerah
p: Jubilees leaves out the scarlet thread of Genesis 38:27-30. Perez is the ancestor of David (Ruth 4:18-22) and of Jesus (Matthew 1:3).
b: Genesis 38:27-30 tells how the twins were born, with the midwife's scarlet thread and Perez's "breach." Jubilees gives only the names and the year: the seventh year of the second week, year 2170 by the book's count. Perez's line led to Boaz and David (Ruth 4:12; Ruth 4:18-22), and Matthew names Tamar in Jesus' family line (Matthew 1:3).

a: he had uncovered his son's robe
p: A Hebrew idiom for sleeping with a close relative's wife, used of a father's wife in Deuteronomy 22:30.
b: The law forbids a man to "uncover the skirt" of his father, meaning to sleep with his father's wife (Deuteronomy 22:30; Deuteronomy 27:20). Jubilees uses the same idiom of Reuben (33:9) and here turns it around: Judah uncovered his son's robe by sleeping with his son's wife (Leviticus 18:15). Charles 1902 (page 230) compares the Testament of Judah 14, "I uncovered the covering of my sons' uncleanness."

a: We told him in a dream that he was forgiven
p: The angels tell Judah in a dream that he is forgiven. Genesis says nothing of Judah's repentance or forgiveness.
b: The "we" is the angels of the presence, who tell the whole story to Moses. Jubilees adds a full repentance to Genesis 38: Judah sees his sin, mourns, pleads with the Lord, and does not repeat it, and God forgives him. Charles 1902 (page 231) compares the Testament of Judah 19, where Judah says God forgave him because he acted in ignorance. Goes beyond the Bible, though the pattern of confession and forgiveness matches Psalm 32:5 and David's repentance in 2 Samuel 12:13.

a: from his ignorance
p: The Ge'ez can mean "from his ignorance" or "because of his ignorance." Charles thought the second was meant.
b: The Ge'ez preposition ʾəm can mean "from" or "because of." Charles 1902 (page 231) argued that the sense should be "forgiven because of his ignorance and because he turned from his sin," as in the Testament of Judah 19, "he forgave because I did it in ignorance." Paul says something similar of himself: mercy was shown to him "because I did it without knowing" (1 Timothy 1:13). The Plain English Translation keeps the order of VanderKam's Ge'ez text.

a: anyone who lies with his mother-in-law, must be burned in fire
p: Leviticus 20:14 sets burning for a man who takes a woman and her mother. Jubilees agrees, and adds the daughter-in-law (41:26).
b: For a man who takes a woman and her mother, Leviticus says, "They are to burn him and them in fire" (Leviticus 20:14). Agrees with that law. For a man who lies with his daughter-in-law, Leviticus 20:12 says "the two of them must be put to death" (Leviticus 20:12) without naming the means; Charles 1902 (page 231) notes this. Jubilees sets burning for that case too (41:26), as Judah's sentence in Genesis 38:24 presupposed. Goes beyond Leviticus there.

a: As for you, command the Israelites
p: The angel turns to Moses and gives a law for Israel. The story of Judah becomes the occasion for it.
b: Jubilees often moves from a story to a law with a direct word to Moses: "As for you, command the Israelites." Here Judah's sin becomes the ground for a law against sleeping with a daughter-in-law or mother-in-law. The promise that God "will turn away anger and punishment from Israel" treats such sins as a danger to the whole people, not just the guilty pair, the same thinking as Numbers 25:11.

a: his two sons had not lain with her
p: Because Er and Onan never consummated their marriages, Tamar was not fully Judah's daughter-in-law, and his line could stand.
b: This verse answers a question Genesis leaves open: how could the line of David come from a union the law calls incest? Jubilees' answer is that Tamar had never truly become the wife of Er or Onan, since neither lay with her in the full sense (41:2; 41:5). So Judah's sin was real but not the worst kind, and his offspring was not cut off. Charles 1902 (page 228) sums up the chapter as Judah forgiven because he sinned in ignorance and repented, and because Tamar's marriage with his sons had not been consummated.

a: with an undivided heart
p: The Ge'ez says Judah acted "in the singleness of his eyes," with honest intent, when he sentenced Tamar.
b: The phrase means sincerity: Judah did not condemn Tamar to cover himself, but because he honestly thought the law required it. Charles 1902 translates "in singleness of eye." Compare Jesus' saying, "If your eye is sound, light will fill your whole body" (Matthew 6:22), where the Greek word for "sound" also means single or sincere. The "command of Abraham" is his charge in 20:4 to burn a woman who commits sexual sin.

a: In the first year of the third week of the forty-fifth jubilee
p: By the book's count this is year 2171 after creation, seven years after the plenty began.
b: Forty-four jubilees (2,156 years), two weeks (14 years) and 1 year make 2171, the figure Charles 1902 prints in his margin. The plenty ended at 41:22, after the twins' birth in 2170.

a: The rain refused to be given to the earth
p: Genesis gives no cause. Jubilees says no rain fell, and in 45:10 that the Nile did not flood.
b: Genesis 41:54 says only that famine came "as Joseph had said." Jubilees gives natural causes: no rain in Canaan and the lands around, and in Egypt a Nile that watered only a few places by its banks (45:10). In Egypt, where it rarely rains, harvests depended on the river's yearly flood. The Bible elsewhere says God withholds rain as a sign or a judgment (Deuteronomy 11:17; 1 Kings 17:1).

a: for gold
p: Genesis says the grain was bought with silver. The Ge'ez word wärq means gold, though Charles sometimes renders it "money."
b: In Genesis the brothers buy grain with silver (Genesis 42:25; Genesis 47:14), the usual Hebrew word for money. The Ge'ez here and throughout these chapters has wärq, gold. Charles's English (1913) gives "gold" in 42:3 and 42:7 and "money" for the same word in 42:12 and 42:25. The Plain English Translation writes "gold" each time.

a: Haven't you come to scout out the ways into the land?
p: Jubilees shortens Genesis 42:7-24: no bowing, no mention of Joseph's dreams, no three days in custody.
b: Genesis 42:6-9 says the brothers bowed with their faces to the ground, and Joseph remembered his dreams. Jubilees leaves out the bowing and the dreams, as it left out the dreams themselves in its account of Joseph's youth. It also omits the brothers' guilty words about Joseph in Genesis 42:21-22, which Reuben answers. What remains is the bare plot.

a: the lord of the country
p: This is the brothers' report in Genesis 42:29-34, in one sentence.
b: Genesis 42:29-34 gives the brothers' whole report again, then the discovery of the silver (Genesis 42:35). Jubilees puts the report in one sentence and has Jacob notice the returned gold only in 42:12.

a: you would bring my old age down to death in grief
p: Genesis 42:38 says Jacob will go down to Sheol. Jubilees says down to death.
b: Jacob says in Genesis, "you will send me down to Sheol, gray-haired and grieving" (Genesis 42:38). Sheol is the Hebrew name for the place of the dead. The Ge'ez has mot, death, here and in Judah's words at 43:12. Jubilees also adds Jacob's fear that the boy might catch a fever on the road, a homely touch.

a: Many of the Egyptians had stored up their grain
p: Jubilees adds that ordinary Egyptians copied Joseph and stored grain, so they lived on their own stores for a year.
b: Genesis 41:55-56 has all Egypt crying to Pharaoh for bread as soon as the famine begins. Jubilees adds that many Egyptians had seen Joseph storing grain and done the same, so they fed themselves for the first year (42:14). It also explains why Joseph had grain to sell to foreigners. Goes beyond the Bible.

a: put my two sons to death in exchange for his life
p: Genesis 42:37 has Reuben make this offer after the first journey. Jubilees moves it to the second, beside Judah's.
b: In Genesis Reuben offers his two sons at once (Genesis 42:37), and Jacob refuses (Genesis 42:38). Only later, when the food runs out, does Judah offer himself (Genesis 43:8-9). Jubilees sets the two offers side by side and has Jacob refuse Reuben and accept Judah. The book gives Judah a place of honor (see 31:18), and his offer prepares for his plea in 43:11-13.

a: stacte, almonds, terebinth nuts and pure honey
p: Genesis 43:11 lists balm, honey, gum, myrrh, pistachios and almonds. Jubilees has four gifts.
b: Jacob's gift in Genesis 43:11 has six items. Jubilees has four. The first Ge'ez item, mayä ləbn, Charles renders "stacte," a fragrant resin. "Terebinth" is a Greek word kept in the Ge'ez (ṭerebentos). Both stacte and terebinth are in the Greek Genesis list (staktē, terebinthos), where the Hebrew has words usually taken as myrrh and pistachios. Jubilees leaves out the double silver of Genesis 43:12 and Jacob's prayer for mercy (Genesis 43:14).
orig: ማየ ፡ ልብን ፡ ወከርካዕ ፡ ወጤሬቤንቶስ ፡ ወጸቃውዐ ፡ መዓር (mayä ləbn wäkärkaʿ wäṭerebentos wäṣäqawʿä mäʿar)

a: in the second year of this week, on the first day of the month
p: By the book's count this is year 2172, the famine's second year (see 43:17).
b: Forty-four jubilees, two weeks and 2 years make 2172. Joseph says in 43:17 that this is the second year of the famine, and Jacob reaches Egypt in this same year, on the first day of the fourth month (45:1). The text does not say which month the brothers set out.

a: He saw his brother Benjamin and recognized him
p: Genesis 43:29-31 has Joseph rush out to weep. Jubilees leaves out his tears here.
b: In Genesis Joseph's heart burns for his brother and he goes into an inner room to weep (Genesis 43:30-31). Jubilees saves Joseph's tears for the moment he makes himself known (43:15). Joseph's blessing, "May the Lord have mercy on you, my son," stands for Genesis 43:29.

a: seven times larger
p: Genesis says Benjamin's portion was five times as large. Jubilees makes it seven.
b: Genesis says "Benjamin's was five times as large as anyone else's" (Genesis 43:34). Jubilees says seven times. Seven is the book's favorite number, built into its weeks, jubilees and Sabbaths. Jubilees also leaves out the seating by age that amazed the brothers (Genesis 43:33) and the Egyptians eating apart (Genesis 43:32).

a: to find out what they were thinking, whether they had peaceful thoughts toward one another
p: Genesis never says why Joseph planted the cup. Jubilees gives his reason: to see whether the brothers were at peace with one another.
b: Readers of Genesis have long asked why Joseph tormented his brothers: revenge, a test of repentance, or a way to bring Benjamin to him? Jubilees answers plainly: he wanted to know if they had "peaceful thoughts" toward one another, that is, whether they would abandon Benjamin as they had abandoned him. The answer comes in 43:14: their hearts were united for good. Brotherly love is a theme Jubilees presses hard (Isaac's charge in 36:4; Israel in Egypt in 46:1).

a: before I go out to my judgment seat
p: Jubilees adds that Joseph was about to sit as judge, which explains his hurry.
b: Genesis 44:4-5 has no such detail. Jubilees gives Joseph a judge's seat, fitting its picture of him as a fair ruler who judged all the people of the land (40:8).

a: We your servants even brought back from the land of Canaan the gold we found in our sacks the first time
p: Verses 4-6 follow Genesis 44:7-10: the returned money as proof, and the offer of death for the thief.
b: The argument is the same as in Genesis 44:8: honest men who brought back money they could have kept would not steal a cup. Jubilees has not told of the money's return earlier, but the brothers mention it here as Genesis does. The steward's answer, that only the guilty man will be a slave, matches Genesis 44:10.

a: Here we are, your servants, our lord's, and our donkeys too
p: In Genesis 44:16 the brothers offer themselves together with the one who had the cup. Jubilees adds their donkeys.
b: Charles 1902 (page 236) notes that Genesis 44:16 has the brothers offer "all of us, along with the one who had the cup in his hand," which stresses their loyalty to Benjamin. Jubilees' brothers offer themselves and their donkeys, and Joseph sends them home without Benjamin (43:10). The loyalty theme comes back fully in Judah's speech (43:11-13).

a: a man takes delight in his cup
p: In Genesis the cup is one Joseph "reads omens with." Jubilees removes the divination.
b: Genesis 44:5 calls the cup the one Joseph drinks from "and what he reads omens with," and in Genesis 44:15 Joseph says a man like him can read omens. The law forbids divination (Deuteronomy 18:10). Jubilees has instead "a man takes delight in his cup." Charles 1902 (page 236) notes that a small change in the Ge'ez verb would give "divines," but that the difference may be deliberate. It fits his description of the book as removing "dogmatically offensive elements" from Genesis (page xiii). Differs from Genesis.

a: I too fear the Lord
p: Joseph said the same on the first journey in Genesis 42:18. Jubilees moves the line here.
b: In Genesis 42:18 Joseph tells his brothers, "I am a man who fears God," as a reason they can trust his terms. In Jubilees he says it while pretending to keep Benjamin. Both times the brothers do not grasp that an Egyptian ruler is speaking of their own God.

a: Please, my lord
p: The Ge'ez literally says "on me, my lord." Charles explained it as a too-literal rendering of the Hebrew bi, "please."
b: Judah begins in Hebrew with bi adoni, "please, my lord" (Genesis 44:18). The word bi looks like "in me" or "on me," and Charles 1902 (page 236) concluded that the Ge'ez "on me" goes back to a translator who took it that way. The Plain English Translation gives the sense Judah's word had.

a: Your servant's mother bore our father two brothers
p: Verses 11-13 condense Judah's long plea in Genesis 44:18-34, the longest speech in Genesis.
b: Judah's plea in Genesis 44:18-34 retells the whole story and ends with his offer to stay as a slave. Jubilees keeps the core: two sons of one mother, one lost, the father's life bound to the boy's, and Judah's pledge. The words "one went away and was lost" keep Jacob's belief from Genesis 44:28 without the torn coat.

a: I stood as his guarantor
p: Judah, who once proposed selling Joseph, now offers to be a slave in Benjamin's place.
b: Read beside Genesis, the change in Judah stands out. In Genesis 37:26-27 he proposed selling Joseph; now he offers his own freedom for Joseph's brother (Genesis 44:33). In Genesis 49:8-10 Judah receives the promise of kingship, and Jubilees already had Isaac bless him as a prince over Jacob's sons (31:18). Jubilees keeps Judah's offer whole, though it shortens almost everything else in Genesis 44.

a: all their hearts were united, each man with his brother, for good
p: Jubilees states the result of Joseph's test (42:25): the brothers were one at heart. Genesis lets the reader infer it.
b: In Genesis 45:1 Joseph simply can no longer control himself. Jubilees adds what he saw: the brothers' hearts were united in goodness. The book values harmony among brothers highly, and it will say that after Jacob's death Israel in Egypt was of one heart, brother loving brother (46:1). Compare Psalm 133:1.

a: He spoke with them in the Hebrew language
p: Genesis says Joseph sent everyone out. Jubilees says he spoke to them in Hebrew, a language the Egyptians would not understand.
b: In Genesis 45:1 Joseph sends the Egyptians out before he reveals himself, and in 42:23 he had used an interpreter. Jubilees has him simply switch to Hebrew. For this book Hebrew is the language of creation, restored to Abraham after Babel (12:25-26). Charles 1902 (page 237) notes that Genesis Rabbah 93 also has Joseph speak Hebrew to his brothers. Jubilees then says the brothers still did not recognize him, perhaps because they could not believe it.

a: the Lord sent me ahead of you to set things in order, so that many people would live
p: This is Joseph's great word in Genesis 45:5-7 and 50:20: God sent him ahead to save lives.
b: Joseph's explanation is the theological center of the Joseph story in Genesis: the brothers meant evil, "but God planned it for good, to do what is happening today: to keep many people alive" (Genesis 50:20). Jubilees keeps it, briefly, and adds that the Lord sent Joseph to "set things in order." Jubilees leaves out the line that the brothers sold Joseph (Genesis 45:4).

a: clothes of many colors
p: Claude's theory: the gift of colored clothes may quietly answer the colored robe that started the trouble.
b: Claude's theory. Genesis 45:22 has Joseph give each brother "a change of clothes." Jubilees says "clothes of many colors" (ḥəbr, color). Many readers and old versions picture Joseph's robe in Genesis 37:3 as many-colored, and the brothers' envy of it began the story. Here Joseph gives all of them colored clothes. Jubilees never mentions the robe in its account of Joseph's youth, so the link, if intended, is left to readers who know Genesis. We have not found this suggested in published scholarship.

a: carts
p: The Ge'ez uses one word, särägälat, for Joseph's chariot (40:6) and for the carts sent for Jacob (43:21, 43:24, 44:7).
b: The same Ge'ez word stands for the "second chariot" Joseph rides in (40:6) and for the vehicles Pharaoh sends to bring Jacob's family (here, 43:24 and 44:7). The Plain English Translation follows the site's Genesis for each: "chariot" for Joseph's (Genesis 41:43) and "carts" for the family's (Genesis 45:21; Genesis 45:27; Genesis 46:5). Charles's English has "chariots" here and "wagons" in 43:24 and 44:7.

a: It is enough for me
p: The Ge'ez says literally "it is great to me," the same words as the Greek of Genesis 45:28.
b: The site's Genesis 45:28 has Israel say "Enough!" The Greek Genesis reads Mega moi estin, "it is great to me," and the Ge'ez has the same words, ʿäbiy wəʾtu litä. Charles 1902 (page 238) notes that the Ge'ez is the literal equivalent of the Greek. It comes back in Jacob's words in 45:4.

a: Israel set out from Haran
p: The Ge'ez says Haran, far to the north. Charles thought it a slip for Hebron, where Jacob lived.
b: Jacob had long since left Haran in Mesopotamia; he was living near Hebron (Genesis 37:14; Genesis 35:27). Charles 1902 (page 238) marked "Haran" as corrupt: it "seems corrupt for 'Hebron,'" which he says is presupposed by 44:6 and by Genesis 37:14. VanderKam's Ge'ez text reads Haran, so the Plain English Translation keeps it.

a: the Well of the Oath
t: The Well of the Oath is Beersheba
p: Jubilees translates the name Beersheba instead of giving it: "well of the oath."
b: Genesis 21:31 explains the name Beersheba: "there the two of them swore an oath" (Genesis 21:31). Hebrew be'er means well and sheva is close to the word for oath. The Ge'ez ʿäzäqtä mäḥäla translates the name, as Jubilees does elsewhere. Abraham and Isaac both worshiped there (Genesis 21:33; Genesis 26:23-25), and in Genesis 46:1 Jacob sacrifices there on his way to Egypt.

a: on the first day of the third month
t: Dated to the Feast of Weeks
p: Jacob leaves on the first of the third month, sacrifices on the seventh, waits seven days, and keeps the festival on the fifteenth.
b: The dates are exact. Jacob leaves on the first day of the third month and offers sacrifice on the seventh. He waits seven days (44:3), keeps the harvest festival (44:4), and on the sixteenth the Lord appears (44:5); he sets out that same day (44:8). Charles 1902 (page 238) concludes that Jacob keeps the Feast of Weeks on the fifteenth of the third month, the date Jubilees gives that feast. Jubilees says the feast was set on the heavenly tablets to renew the covenant every year (6:17).

a: Jacob remembered the dream he had seen at Bethel
p: Genesis gives no reason for Jacob's fear, only God's "Do not be afraid" in 46:3. Jubilees points back to Bethel.
b: At Bethel God promised to bring Jacob back to this land (Genesis 28:15; 27:24), and in a later Bethel vision an angel showed him seven tablets of what would happen to him and his sons (32:21-22). Leaving Canaan might seem to break the promise, or Jacob might remember that his descendants would be oppressed in a foreign land (Genesis 15:13). Jubilees does not say which. God's answer in 44:6 covers both: "I will bring you up again."

a: He kept the harvest festival, the first crops of the grain, with old grain
t: The Feast of Weeks kept in famine
p: Exodus 23:16 calls it the Feast of Harvest; Exodus 34:22 the Feast of Weeks. Jacob keeps it with old grain, because nothing grew.
b: Exodus names the feast both ways: "the Feast of Harvest, for the first crops of your work" (Exodus 23:16) and "the Feast of Weeks, with the first crops of the wheat harvest" (Exodus 34:22). Jubilees calls it a double feast, of weeks and of first fruits (6:21). Here there is no harvest, so Jacob offers old grain. The Ge'ez sərnay is wheat, or grain in general (Dillmann's Lexicon linguae aethiopicae). Goes beyond the Bible: Genesis 46:1 says only that he offered sacrifices at Beersheba. For Jubilees the point is that the feast was kept even by the fathers and even in famine.
orig: በዓለ ፡ ማእረር ፡ ቀዳሜ ፡ ፍሬ ፡ ስርናይ (bäʿalä maʾrär qädame fəre sərnay)

a: I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and Isaac
p: Genesis 46:2-4 in Jubilees' words. Genesis says "the God of your father"; Jubilees names Abraham and Isaac.
b: Genesis 46:2 says God spoke "in visions at night"; Jubilees says the Lord appeared, after seven days of waiting. The call "Jacob, Jacob" and the answer "Here I am" match Genesis 46:2. Genesis has "the God of your father"; Jubilees widens it to "the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and Isaac," the form God uses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:6).

a: Joseph will lay his hand on your eyes
p: To close a dying man's eyes was a son's last duty. God promises Jacob that Joseph will be there at his death.
b: Genesis 46:4 has the same promise. Jubilees adds "In this land you will be buried," which seems to mean Canaan, "this land" where God speaks, since Jacob is in fact buried at Hebron (45:15). Charles 1902 (page 239) notes that the Ge'ez verb for "bring you up" here has an unusual sense, like the Greek "lead up."

a: to look over the land of Goshen
t: "To look over" or "to show the way"?
p: The Hebrew of Genesis 46:28 says Judah was sent "to point the way." Jubilees agrees with the Samaritan, Greek and Syriac "to see."
b: The site's Genesis 46:28 says Jacob sent Judah "to point the way before him to Goshen" (Genesis 46:28), following the Masoretic Hebrew lehorot. Charles 1902 (page 239) notes that the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint and the Syriac presuppose lir'ot, "to see," and that the Targum Onkelos has much the same. (Swete's Greek has "to meet him.") Jubilees agrees with that group.

a: Here are the names of Jacob's sons who went into Egypt
p: Verses 11-34 retell Genesis 46:8-27, but count the seventy differently.
b: The list follows the order of Genesis 46: Leah's sons, Zilpah's, Rachel's, then Bilhah's. Many names match. But Jubilees gives Dan five sons and Naphtali five, leaves out Er and Onan and Perez's sons from the count, and drops Asher's grandsons. It includes Jacob in the seventy (see the note on 44:33). The names are given here in their Genesis forms where they match; the Ge'ez forms, many of them from the Greek, are given in the notes.

a: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron and Carmi
p: The Ge'ez spells Hanoch exactly like Enoch, and Pallu and Hezron in Greek forms.
b: The Ge'ez has ʾEnok, Falus, ʾEsrom and Karami. ʾEnok is the same name as Enoch (Hebrew Hanokh), and Falus and ʾEsrom come from the Greek forms of Pallu and Hezron. Charles 1902 (page 240) lists the Ge'ez forms. Reuben, his four sons, makes five.
orig: ኤኖክ ፡ ወፋሉስ ፡ ወኤስሮም ፡ ወከራሚ (ʾenok wäfalus wäʾesrom wäkärami)

a: Shelah, Perez and Zerah, four
p: Genesis 46:12 lists Er and Onan, though dead, and Perez's sons Hezron and Hamul. Jubilees counts only the living sons.
b: Genesis 46:12 names all five of Judah's sons, notes that Er and Onan died in Canaan, and adds two grandsons. Jubilees counts Judah and three sons as four, and tells of Er and Onan separately in 44:34. Charles 1902 (page 239) shows how this changes the total.

a: Tola, Puvah, Jashub and Shimron
p: Genesis 46:13 in Hebrew names Issachar's third son Iob. Jubilees has Jashub, with the Samaritan and Greek Genesis.
b: The site's Genesis 46:13 has "Tola, Puvah, Iob and Shimron," following the Masoretic Hebrew. The Ge'ez has Iyasub, that is Jashub, the form in Numbers 26:24 and 1 Chronicles 7:1. Charles 1902 (page 240) notes that the Samaritan Pentateuch of Genesis 46:13 reads Jashub; the Septuagint has a similar form (Iasouph in Swete's text).

a: in Mesopotamia
p: Genesis 46:15 says Paddan-aram. Jubilees uses the Greek name Mesopotamia, "between the rivers."
b: Paddan-aram, "the plain of Aram," was the region around Haran. The Greek Genesis usually renders it Mesopotamia, and the Ge'ez form Mäsp̣eṭomya comes from the Greek. Leah's group here is twenty-nine, thirty with Jacob; Genesis 46:15 counts thirty-three.

a: five
p: Each total in this list counts the father with his children. Asher's "five" does not, so it is one short.
b: Reuben and his four sons are "five" (44:12), Simeon and his six sons "seven" (44:13), Gad and his seven sons "eight" (44:20). Asher has five children named here, so with Asher the total would be six. Charles's text has "six," and only with six does Zilpah's side make the fourteen of 44:22. VanderKam's Ge'ez as printed says "five"; see the variant on this verse.

a: the daughter of Potiphar, priest of Heliopolis
p: The Ge'ez spells the name Futira, close to Genesis's Potiphera. Jubilees treats him as Potiphar (40:10).
b: The name of Asenath's father varies in the Ge'ez: Faṭifaran (39:2), Fuṭifaran (40:10), and here Fuṭiraʿ, which is close to Genesis's Potiphera (Genesis 41:45). Because Jubilees counts Joseph's master and his father-in-law as one man (see 40:10), the Plain English Translation uses Potiphar for all three. Joseph and his two sons make three.

a: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim and Ard
p: Some of these Ge'ez names are badly garbled. They are given here in the Genesis forms Charles matched them to.
b: The Ge'ez list reads Bala, Bakor, Asbil, Guad, Neʾeman, Abyod, Raʾe, Senanim, Afim and Gaʾam. Charles 1902 (page 241) matched them to the ten sons of Genesis 46:21 and judged the sixth, eighth and tenth "corrupted almost beyond the possibility of recognition." The Plain English Translation uses the Genesis names. Benjamin and ten sons make eleven.
orig: ባላ ፡ ወባኮር ፡ ወአስቢል ፡ ጉአድ ፡ ወንኤማን ፡ ወአብዮድ ፡ ወራኤ ፡ ወሰናኒም ፡ ወአፊም ፡ ወጋአም (bala wäbakor wäʾäsbil guʾäd wänʾeman wäʾäbyod wäraʾe wäsänanim wäʾäfim wägaʾäm)

a: Hushim, Samon, Asudi, Iyaka and Salomon, six
p: Genesis 46:23 gives Dan one son, Hushim. Jubilees gives him five, four of whom died in Egypt that same year.
b: Genesis 46:23 reads in Hebrew "the sons of Dan: Hushim," a plural with one name. Charles 1902 (page 241) notes that the Targum called Pseudo-Jonathan says Dan's sons were beyond counting, and that the Talmud (Bava Batra 143b, as quoted by Beer) says the same. Jubilees solves the plural its own way: Dan had five sons, but four died in Egypt in the year they arrived (44:29), leaving Hushim. Goes beyond the Bible.

a: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer, Shallum and Iv
p: Jubilees' Jahziel and Shallum match 1 Chronicles 7:13, not Genesis 46:24. The fifth son, Iv, is not in Genesis.
b: The site's Genesis 46:24 has "Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer and Shillem." Charles 1902 (page 241) notes that Jubilees' forms Jahziel and Shallum agree with 1 Chronicles 7:13 instead, and that Iv is not in Genesis at all. Jubilees adds that Iv was born after the years of famine and died in Egypt (44:31), yet the list still counts him: with Naphtali's five sons, Bilhah's side makes twelve (44:32), and the total of seventy (44:33) needs him. How a son born after the famine could be among those who went down, the text does not say. Charles gives no explanation; his note says only "Not in Gen. xlvi. 24."
orig: ኢያሲኤል ፡ ወጋሂኒ ፡ ወአሰአር ፡ ወሰሉም ፡ ወኤው (ʾiyasiʾel wägahini wäʾäsäʾär wäsälum wäʾew)

a: All those of Rachel were twenty-six
p: Rachel's own children (fourteen) and those of her servant Bilhah (twelve) make twenty-six.
b: Leah's side is forty-four: her own thirty with Jacob (44:18) and Zilpah's fourteen (44:22). Rachel's side is twenty-six: her own fourteen (44:26) and Bilhah's twelve, Dan and Naphtali with five sons each. Forty-four and twenty-six make seventy.

a: were seventy persons
p: Genesis counts seventy, the Greek Genesis and Acts 7:14 seventy-five. Jubilees counts seventy, including Jacob.
b: Genesis 46:26-27 counts sixty-six who went down, then seventy with Joseph, his two sons and Jacob; Exodus 1:5 and Deuteronomy 10:22 say seventy. The Septuagint of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 reads seventy-five, adding Joseph's grandsons, and Stephen follows it: "seventy-five people" (Acts 7:14). Charles 1902 (page 239) works out Jubilees' sum: Leah's side 29, Zilpah's 14, Rachel's 14, Bilhah's 12, which is 69, plus Jacob makes 70. Agrees with Genesis on seventy but reaches it by a different list. Seventy is also the number of the nations (44:34; Genesis 10).

a: they were counted among the seventy nations
t: Er and Onan among the nations
p: A hard line. "They were counted among the seventy nations" can be read of Er and Onan, or of Israel.
b: Charles renders it "reckoned among the seventy Gentile nations." The nations of the world number seventy in the table of Genesis 10, and Jubilees divides the earth among them (8-9). The Ge'ez does not say who "they" are, and two readings are possible. First, Er and Onan, who died for their sins and left no heirs, are not counted among Israel's seventy souls but are reckoned with the nations. Second, the subject is the Israelites of the same sentence, or the seventy just listed: Israel's seventy souls are reckoned as matching the seventy nations of the world. Charles gives no explanation, and the Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez as open as it is.
orig: ወተሠይሙ ፡ ውስተ ፡ ሰብዓ ፡ ሕዝብ (wätäśäymu wəstä säbʿa ḥəzb)

a: they were counted among the seventy nations
t: Er among the nations he wanted
p: Claude's theory: if the line means Er and Onan, Er ends up counted with the very nations he wanted to marry into.
b: Claude's theory. On the first reading of this line, Er and Onan are reckoned with the nations, not with Israel. Jubilees said that Er would not lie with Tamar because he wanted a wife from his mother's Canaanite people (41:2). Counted among the nations, he would end where his wish pointed. This rests only on 41:2 and 44:34 read together; we have not found the link made in the sources read for this part.

a: on the first day of the fourth month
p: The first day of the fourth month is one of the four "days of remembrance" in Jubilees' calendar (6:23).
b: Jubilees' 364-day year has four quarters, each opened by a day of remembrance: the first days of the first, fourth, seventh and tenth months (6:23). Jacob enters Egypt on one of them, in year 2172 by the book's count (forty-four jubilees, two weeks, two years). He left Beersheba on the sixteenth of the third month (44:8), so the journey took about two weeks.

a: He fell on his father's neck and wept
p: Genesis 46:29 has Joseph weep on his father's neck "a long while."
b: The reunion follows Genesis 46:28-30. Jubilees leaves out Joseph's chariot and his plan to present the brothers as shepherds (Genesis 46:31-47:6), and Jacob's meeting with Pharaoh, where he blesses the king (Genesis 47:7-10).

a: who has not held back his mercy and his kindness from his servant Jacob
p: Genesis gives Jacob one sentence. Jubilees gives him a prayer of praise.
b: In Genesis 46:30 Jacob says only that he can die now, having seen Joseph alive. Jubilees adds a blessing of "the God of Israel, the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac." Abraham's servant praised God in similar words, "who has not stopped showing his loyal love and faithfulness" (Genesis 24:27). Goes beyond the Bible.

a: while I am alive
t: "While I am alive" or "while you are alive"?
p: Genesis 46:30 has "that you are still alive." The Ge'ez has "while I am alive." Charles thought one letter had changed.
b: Jacob's words in Genesis are "after seeing your face, that you are still alive" (Genesis 46:30). The Ge'ez reads ʾənzä ḥəyaw ʾänä, "while I am alive." Charles 1902 (page 242) marked "I am" as probably corrupt: changing Ge'ez ʾänä "I" to ʾantä "you" would match Genesis. Both make sense, and VanderKam's text reads "I," so the Plain English Translation keeps it.

a: the vision I saw at Bethel is true
p: At Bethel God promised to be with Jacob and bring him back. Seeing Joseph alive, Jacob says the vision has proved true.
b: Genesis 28:15 promised, "Look, I am with you. I will guard you everywhere you go." Jubilees told of Jacob's fear at the thought of leaving Canaan (44:2). Now he declares the Bethel vision true. It may also mean the later Bethel vision of seven tablets, which showed him what would happen to his sons (32:21).

a: He blessed the Creator of all things
p: Jacob blesses God for keeping all twelve sons. Jubilees ends the family's division with a shared meal.
b: Genesis has no such meal with Jacob present. Jubilees makes the family reunion complete: Joseph eats and drinks with the brothers who sold him, in front of their father, and Jacob blesses God who kept all twelve. The title "Creator of all" is common in later Jewish prayer and in Jubilees. Goes beyond the Bible.

a: a hundred and thirty years old
p: Genesis 47:9 has Jacob tell Pharaoh he is a hundred and thirty. Jubilees states it without the meeting with Pharaoh.
b: Genesis 47:9 puts the number in Jacob's mouth, with his sad words about his few and evil years. Jubilees keeps only the number. The land given is "Goshen and Rameses," as in Genesis 47:11; Charles 1902 (page 242) notes that the Ge'ez form Ramesena comes from the Hebrew.

a: with as much bread as they could eat
p: Genesis 47:12 measures the food by the little ones. Charles thought the Ge'ez once matched the Greek "by their persons."
b: The Hebrew of Genesis 47:12 measures the food by the mouths of the little ones: "down to the youngest mouths" (Genesis 47:12). Charles 1902 (page 243) suggests that a slightly different Ge'ez reading would give "according to their persons," as in the Greek Genesis. VanderKam's text reads "as much as eats them," that is, as much as they needed.

a: Joseph acquired the whole land of Egypt for Pharaoh
p: Genesis 47:13-26 tells how Joseph bought Egypt's livestock, land and people for Pharaoh. Jubilees compresses it into one verse.
b: Genesis 47:13-26 is a hard passage for many readers: in exchange for food Joseph acquires the people's money, livestock, land and finally their bodies for Pharaoh. Some readers praise his management; others see the start of the slavery Israel itself would suffer in Egypt (Exodus 1:11-14). Jubilees, which presents Joseph as a perfect ruler (40:8), keeps the outcome and drops the people's pleading. Genesis 47:25 has them say "You have kept us alive!"

a: because the river had flooded the whole land of Egypt
p: Egypt's harvest depended on the Nile's yearly flood. Jubilees says the famine ended when the river rose again.
b: In ancient Egypt the Nile rose each summer and covered the fields with water and fresh soil; when the flood was low, the harvest failed. Jubilees explains the famine and its end in these terms (45:10). Genesis says only that the seven years came to an end. The Bible speaks of the Nile's rise and fall in Amos 8:8 and Amos 9:5.

a: That year was the first year of the fourth week of the forty-fifth jubilee
p: Year 2178 by the book's count, the eighth year after the famine began in 2171.
b: Forty-four jubilees (2,156 years), three weeks (21 years) and 1 year make 2178. The famine began in 2171 (42:1) and ran seven years, so 2178 is the "eighth year" of 45:9. The arithmetic is consistent, as it usually is in Jubilees.

a: Joseph made it a rule for the land of Egypt that stands to this day
p: Genesis 47:24-26 sets the same rule: a fifth of the harvest to Pharaoh, four-fifths to the people.
b: Genesis 47:26 says Joseph "made this the rule for the land of Egypt, and it stands to this day," and that only the priests' land was exempt. Jubilees keeps the rule and the phrase "to this day," now spoken by the angel to Moses. It leaves out the exemption for Egypt's priests.

a: three jubilees, a hundred and forty-seven years
p: Genesis 47:28 gives Jacob a hundred and forty-seven years. In Jubilees that is exactly three jubilees of forty-nine years.
b: Three times forty-nine is a hundred and forty-seven, so Jacob's life in Genesis fits Jubilees' calendar exactly. He dies in year 2188 by the book's count (forty-four jubilees, four weeks, four years). Charles 1902 (page 244) notes that this date conflicts with the date of Jacob's birth given in 19:13, which would make his death year 2193; the book's numbers do not always agree.

a: what would come on them in the last days
p: This is Genesis 49, the blessing of the twelve sons, in one sentence: "what will meet you in the last days" (Genesis 49:1).
b: Genesis 49:1 opens Jacob's last words: "I will tell you what will meet you in the last days" (Genesis 49:1). Jubilees adds that he also told them what would happen "in the land of Egypt," the slavery to come. It does not give the blessings themselves, perhaps because it has already given Isaac's blessings of Levi and Judah (31:13-20) and does not repeat Genesis 49's harsh words about Simeon and Levi (Genesis 49:5-7).

a: he gave Joseph two portions in the land
p: Genesis 48:22 has "one shoulder of land" (shekem, also the name Shechem). Jubilees says two portions, the firstborn's double share.
b: In Genesis 48:22 Jacob gives Joseph "one shoulder of land" above his brothers; the Hebrew shekem is also the name of the town Shechem, where Joseph was later buried (Joshua 24:32). Jubilees says two portions, matching the firstborn's "double share" (Deuteronomy 21:17) and the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh (Genesis 48:5). Charles 1902 (page 244) links the verse to Genesis 48:22.

a: the double cave in the land of Canaan
p: Genesis's Machpelah may mean "double." The Greek Genesis already calls it "the double cave."
b: Abraham bought "the cave of Machpelah" as a family grave (Genesis 23:9). The Greek Genesis translates the name as to spēlaion to diploun, "the double cave," and the Ge'ez takes the same picture. Jacob is buried "near Abraham his father," as Genesis 49:29-31 and 50:13 say. Stephen in Acts says the patriarchs "were moved to Shechem" (Acts 7:16), a different tradition; Jubilees, like Genesis, puts Jacob at Hebron and the other sons there later (46:9).

a: the grave he had dug for himself
p: Genesis 50:5 has Joseph tell Pharaoh that Jacob made him swear to bury him "in my grave, the one I dug for myself."
b: Jubilees puts the detail in the narrator's voice, from Genesis 50:5. It leaves out the long funeral procession to Canaan and the Egyptians' mourning (Genesis 50:1-14), and Joseph's oath (Genesis 47:29-31).

a: He gave all his books, and the books of his fathers, to his son Levi
p: Jubilees says Jacob handed the family's books to Levi to keep and copy. This claims that Israel's priests guard the oldest learning.
b: Jubilees pictures a chain of written knowledge from the beginning: Enoch writes (4:17-19), Noah gives his books to Shem (10:14), Jacob reads Abraham's words (39:6), and now the books pass to Levi, whom Isaac had blessed as priest (31:13-17). The verb "renew" (ḥädäsä) is used of copying a book out afresh: Dillmann's Lexicon linguae aethiopicae gives that sense and cites this very verse. "To this day" means Moses' day, and by implication the writer's. Charles 1902 (page 244) inferred that the author, who claims to hand on these traditions, "was a descendant of Levi, and probably a priest." In the 66 books the priests also keep the law: Moses gives it to them (Deuteronomy 31:9), and "the lips of a priest keep knowledge safe" (Malachi 2:7). Goes beyond the Bible: no book of the Bible speaks of writings of the patriarchs.
